messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Police Officer
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 77

He is 18 now, a young African man in a police uniform that still looks slightly too stiff on his body, as if he has stepped into adulthood before he has fully grown into it. When he talks about why he joined the police, he first says what people often say—that he wants to protect others, that he wants to serve. Only after several conversations does the deeper story emerge, and when it does, it comes not as a neat explanation but in fragments: the sound of a chair scraping across concrete, his mother’s breath catching, a bottle breaking against the wall, the feeling of standing frozen in a dark doorway as a boy.

He grows up in a small crowded home where evenings are unpredictable. During the day, there are ordinary things—school uniforms drying on a line, neighbors calling out to one another, his mother humming while cooking. But once his father begins drinking, the atmosphere changes. Even before any shouting starts, he can feel it in his stomach. As a child, he learns to read tiny signals: the heaviness of his father’s footsteps, the way his mother’s shoulders tense, the silence that settles over the room like everyone is holding their breath at once.

The worst nights stay with him in pieces rather than full memories. He remembers seeing his father strike his mother hard enough that she falls against the table. He remembers wanting to run forward and not moving. He remembers his younger siblings crying and looking at him as if he should know what to do. On one night he still revisits in his mind, he stands between the bedroom and the main room, watching his father kick at the door after his mother locks it. He is sure she is going to die. He can still recall the pounding in his ears, so loud it drowns out everything else. Afterward, when the house finally goes quiet, he does not sleep. He lies awake listening for movement, convinced that if he lets himself drift off, something terrible will happen and he will miss the chance to stop it.

As he gets older, he tells himself he should have done more. Even as a child, he carries a grown man’s guilt. He begins moving through life as if danger is always close. At school, he startles when classmates raise their voices. If teachers ask him why he is tired, he shrugs. He becomes watchful, serious, unusually controlled. Other boys joke and wander; he sits where he can see the door. He does not bring friends home. He is ashamed of the chaos in his house and ashamed, too, of his fear.

When he leaves home, he imagines distance will settle something inside him. Instead, the old fear travels with him. Joining the police gives structure to his vigilance. He tells me that on patrol he feels useful because he is finally the one moving toward trouble instead of standing helpless in a doorway. He is quick to notice changes in tone, posture, and sound. Colleagues praise him for being alert, but inside, alertness does not feel like a skill. It feels compulsory. His body rarely unclenches.

Domestic disturbance calls are the hardest. Even before arriving, his chest tightens. If he hears a woman crying behind a door or the crash of objects inside a house, his mind is no longer fully in the present. He sees his mother. He feels again the sickening certainty that violence is about to erupt. He becomes flooded—heart racing, palms sweating, jaw locked. After these calls, he cannot easily come down. He replays what he saw, then what he saw years ago, the scenes overlapping until he cannot separate one from the other.

At night, sleep is thin and broken. He has dreams in which he is back in the hallway as a child, trying to shout but unable to make a sound. Sometimes he wakes already on his feet, scanning the room before he fully knows where he is. He avoids alcohol because he cannot tolerate the smell on another person’s breath, yet he says little about why. Loud arguments in public make him leave abruptly. When neighbors quarrel, he feels anger surge through him so fast it frightens him. He knows people see him as calm, but the calm is hard-won and brittle.

He has never had an easy romantic relationship. If someone raises their voice, even in frustration, he shuts down or leaves. He wants closeness, but closeness feels dangerous because it means exposure to another person’s moods, another person’s power to turn a room unsafe. He keeps his phone on at night and checks locks repeatedly. He scans exits in restaurants, sits facing the entrance, and notices everyone who walks in. He is exhausted by this and also afraid of what would happen if he stopped.

What troubles him most is not only the fear, but the persistence of the child’s belief that he failed. He speaks of his mother with tenderness and of himself, then and now, with harshness. In his mind, the past is not finished. It returns in sounds, in calls over the radio, in the split second before entering a home where voices are raised. He is a police officer now, but part of him is still that boy in the doorway, bracing for the next blow, waiting for the night to decide how bad it will become.
